title: Your why
hookLine: why practice at all? the Talmud says start even for the wrong reason, and Akiva's story shows why (Pesachim 50b)
tomorrow: Ray says Zoe's morning coffee is already a practice. is it?

lines: EVEN NOT FOR ITS OWN SAKE.
cards: People start running for a wedding photo, or go to services to keep a parent happy. Is that cheating? The Talmud has a line that sounds almost backwards.

Rav Yehuda, in the name of his teacher Rav, says: a person should always busy himself with Torah and good deeds, even not for their own sake. Even for the wrong reason. Isn't the reason the whole point?
Here's the puzzle, and the line's own second half solves it.

teach.h: OUT OF NOT FOR ITS OWN SAKE...
teach.b: Because, the line goes on, out of not for its own sake comes for its own sake. In Hebrew, lishmah: doing the thing for the thing itself, for God and the good, not for praise or reward. Lishmah is the goal.
But the rabbis didn't make it the starting line. So you start where you are, and the practice does some of the work on your heart. Tradition tells it about Rabbi Akiva.

He was an unlearned shepherd, working for a rich man of Jerusalem, Ben Kalba Savua. His daughter, whom later tradition names Rachel, saw something in him. She said she'd marry him if he went to study Torah.
So the man who couldn't read went to the house of study, at least partly for her.

Another story says that, before he started, he watched water dripping on a stone until it had worn a hollow, and thought: if soft water can carve stone, words of Torah can carve a heart. He became a great teacher.
A beginning that was partly for love of Rachel became a life given to Torah for its own sake.
Here's the teaching, plainly: in Jewish tradition you don't wait for a pure motive before you act.
You act, and let the doing grow the motive.
So write your why honestly, even if it's mixed. Then watch where it goes.

how: Jewish teachers cite the Talmud's 'from not for its own sake comes for its own sake' to encourage people to begin study and mitzvot before their motives are pure; lishmah, for its own sake, remains the goal.

o: the honest reason you practice, even if it's mixed
a perfect motive you must have before you begin
a reason someone else gives you for practicing

games.q: the rabbis on your why: tap the pairs.
p: start even for the wrong reason
would marry Akiva if he went to study
words of Torah carve a heart

s: the rabbis taught that a good deed done for the wrong reason is worthless
Rav taught to do it anyway, because out of not for its own sake comes for its own sake.
tradition says Akiva began studying as a grown man who couldn't read
he was a shepherd, and Rachel's condition sent him to the house of study.
in Jewish teaching, the goal is still to act for its own sake
lishmah is where the path aims, even if it doesn't begin there.

games.q: your brother starts volunteering at a food bank mostly because it looks good on applications. your mom says that ruins it. what fits the rabbis' teaching?
o: let him start; doing it for a mixed reason can grow into doing it for its own sake.
she's right; if his reason isn't pure, the volunteering doesn't count.
reasons never matter at all, so there's nothing to grow into.
games.why: Rav says do good even not for its own sake, because that's the road to for its own sake. Lishmah is the goal, not the entry ticket.

practice: Write one honest line: why practice at all? If the true answer is mixed, to sleep better, to feel less alone, to impress someone, write that. Underneath, leave one blank line for the reason you hope it grows into.

wordCard.voice: Your why: the honest reason you practice, mixed or not, which the rabbis say can grow into lishmah, for its own sake.

orig.note: Hebrew: for its own sake; doing Torah and good deeds for the thing itself.

carryVoice: Your line: my why. Akiva started partly for Rachel, and stayed for the Torah. Day 1591, done.

sources.ref: Babylonian Talmud, Pesachim 50b (Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav: one should always engage in Torah and mitzvot even not for their own sake, for out of not for its own sake comes for its own sake)
